items.title: Lesson 25: Time-Based Autoscaling with KEDA Cron Scaler & Multi-Trigger Composition
path: Lesson 25: Time-Based Autoscaling with KEDA Cron Scaler & Multi-Trigger Composition

items.title: 1. Why Time-Based (Cron) Autoscaling?
items.text:
Standard autoscaling is reactive: it detects increased CPU, memory, or queue depth after traffic arrives and takes several minutes to provision new pods and warm application caches.

For many real-world businesses, traffic patterns are highly predictable: - Enterprise SaaS: Heavy usage between 8:00 AM and 6:00 PM on weekdays; minimal usage on weekends. - FinTech / Trading: Massive surges at market opening bell (e.g., 9:15 AM). - E-Commerce: Pre-scheduled flash sales, promotional campaigns, or marketing email blasts. - Batch Processing Windows: Nightly ETL data pipelines between 1:00 AM and 4:00 AM.

The KEDA Cron Scaler enables proactive pre-warming: scaling up capacity before the traffic spike hits so that latency remains flat.

graph TD
    subgraph TimeSchedule["Time & Schedule Triggers"]
        CronDay["Cron Trigger (08:00 - 18:00 Mon-Fri)\nDesired Replicas: 10"]
        CronNight["Off-Hours (18:00 - 08:00 & Weekends)\nDesired Replicas: 0 or 1"]
    end

    subgraph ReactiveMetrics["Reactive Metric Triggers"]
        Prom["Prometheus Trigger (HTTP RPS)\n1 Pod per 100 RPS"]
    end

    CronDay --> Evaluator["KEDA Multi-Trigger Evaluator\nRule: Evaluates MAX(Trigger Replicas)"]
    ReactiveMetrics --> Evaluator
    Evaluator --> Target["Target Workload (Deployment / Rollout)"]
path: Lesson 25: Time-Based Autoscaling with KEDA Cron Scaler & Multi-Trigger Composition

items.title: 2. Anatomy of the KEDA cron Scaler
items.text:
The cron scaler defines a time window during which a specific replica count must be active:

triggers:
  - type: cron
    metadata:
      timezone: America/New_York       # Standard IANA Timezone name
      start: 0 8 * * 1-5               # 8:00 AM Monday through Friday
      end: 0 18 * * 1-5                # 6:00 PM Monday through Friday
      desiredReplicas: '15'            # Target replica count during active window
path: Lesson 25: Time-Based Autoscaling with KEDA Cron Scaler & Multi-Trigger Composition

items.title: Key Parameters:
items.text:
• timezone: Must be a valid IANA Timezone string (e.g., UTC, America/Chicago, Europe/London, Asia/Kolkata). Never rely on node server system clocks.
  • start: Standard 5-field cron expression for when the scaling window opens.
  • end: Standard 5-field cron expression for when the scaling window closes.
  • desiredReplicas: Number of pods to maintain while the current time falls between start and end.

Understanding Cron Active Windows

The active window is defined as the time between start and end. While active, the cron scaler reports desiredReplicas. When outside the active window, the scaler reports 0 (or hands over evaluation to other triggers).
path: Lesson 25: Time-Based Autoscaling with KEDA Cron Scaler & Multi-Trigger Composition

items.title: 3. Multi-Trigger Composition & Evaluation Rules
items.text: In production, you rarely rely solely on Cron or solely on reactive metrics. You combine them!
path: Lesson 25: Time-Based Autoscaling with KEDA Cron Scaler & Multi-Trigger Composition

items.title: How KEDA Resolves Multiple Triggers
items.text:
When multiple triggers are declared inside a single ScaledObject, KEDA calculates the desired replicas for each trigger independently and applies the MAXIMUM value:

\[\text{Final Desired Replicas} = \max(\text{Trigger}_1, \text{Trigger}_2, \dots, \text{Trigger}_n)\]
path: Lesson 25: Time-Based Autoscaling with KEDA Cron Scaler & Multi-Trigger Composition

items.title: Scenario Example:
items.text:
1. At 7:55 AM (Night):
  2. Cron Trigger: Inactive (0 desired pods).
  3. Prometheus Trigger: Low traffic (1 desired pod).
  4. Result: Max(0, 1) = 1 Pod (Cost savings).
  5. At 8:01 AM (Business Day Starts):
  6. Cron Trigger: Active (10 desired pods).
  7. Prometheus Trigger: Low morning traffic (2 desired pods).
  8. Result: Max(10, 2) = 10 Pods (Pre-warmed and ready for users).
  9. At 2:00 PM (Unexpected Mid-Day Surge):
  10. Cron Trigger: Active (10 desired pods).
  11. Prometheus Trigger: 2,500 RPS spike (\(\lceil 2500 / 100 \rceil = 25\) desired pods).
  12. Result: Max(10, 25) = 25 Pods (Burst capacity handles surge).
path: Lesson 25: Time-Based Autoscaling with KEDA Cron Scaler & Multi-Trigger Composition

items.title: 4. Production Blueprint: Pre-Warming + Real-Time Bursts
items.text:
Here is an enterprise-grade ScaledObject combining timezone-aware pre-warming with reactive Prometheus scaling and fallback protection:

apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata:
  name: billing-api-scaler
  namespace: finance
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: billing-api
  minReplicaCount: 1                  # Minimum baseline off-peak
  maxReplicaCount: 40                 # Absolute ceiling during extreme events
  pollingInterval: 15
  cooldownPeriod: 180
  fallback:
    failureThreshold: 3
    replicas: 5                       # Safe fallback if Prometheus fails
  triggers:
    # Trigger 1: Business Hours Pre-Warming (8 AM to 6 PM EST, Mon-Fri)
    - type: cron
      name: business-hours-schedule
      metadata:
        timezone: America/New_York
        start: 0 8 * * 1-5
        end: 0 18 * * 1-5
        desiredReplicas: '12'

    # Trigger 2: Reactive Traffic Bursting via Prometheus
    - type: prometheus
      name: http-rps-burst
      metadata:
        serverAddress: http://prometheus-operated.monitoring.svc:9090
        metricName: billing_http_rps
        query: sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="billing-api"}[2m]))
        threshold: '80'               # 1 pod per 80 RPS
        activationThreshold: '10'
path: Lesson 25: Time-Based Autoscaling with KEDA Cron Scaler & Multi-Trigger Composition

items.title: Test Your Knowledge
items.text:
1. If a ScaledObject has a Cron trigger requesting 10 replicas and a Prometheus trigger requesting 18 replicas, what replica count will KEDA enforce?
  2. A) It selects the maximum value of 18 replicas across active triggers
  3. B) It selects the average value of 14 replicas between both triggers

Answer: A) It selects the maximum value of 18 replicas across active triggers - Correct! KEDA evaluates all declared triggers concurrently and always chooses the highest replica count calculated.

  1. Why is configuring explicit IANA timezone values essential when writing KEDA cron triggers?
  2. A) It guarantees scheduled execution aligns with business working hours
  3. B) It forces worker nodes to synchronize their hardware BIOS clocks

Answer: A) It guarantees scheduled execution aligns with business working hours - Correct! Cluster nodes frequently run in UTC, so specifying IANA timezones (like America/New_York) ensures schedules accurately reflect local business hours.
path: Lesson 25: Time-Based Autoscaling with KEDA Cron Scaler & Multi-Trigger Composition

items.title: Lesson 26: Solving the GitOps Tug-of-War: KEDA + Argo CD Drift & Conflict Resolution
path: Lesson 26: Solving the GitOps Tug-of-War: KEDA + Argo CD Drift & Conflict Resolution

items.title: 1. The GitOps Tug-of-War Dilemma
items.text:
When integrating KEDA (or any Kubernetes autoscaler) into a GitOps workflow with Argo CD, a critical architectural conflict arises: the Replicas Tug-of-War.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Git as Git Repository (spec.replicas: 2)
    participant Argo as Argo CD Controller (Self-Heal: True)
    participant K8s as Kubernetes API (Live State)
    participant KEDA as KEDA Operator (External Queue Spike)

    Note over Git,K8s: Initial State: 2 Replicas Synced
    KEDA->>K8s: Queue depth surges! Scale replicas 2 → 20
    Note over K8s: Live Deployment now has 20 Pods
    Argo->>K8s: Poll live state & compare with Git
    Note over Argo: Drift Detected! Git=2, Live=20 (OutOfSync)
    Argo->>K8s: Self-Heal: Overwrite replicas 20 → 2!
    Note over K8s: 18 active pods abruptly TERMINATED under heavy load!
    KEDA->>K8s: Queue still full! Re-scale replicas 2 → 20
    Note over Argo,KEDA: Destructive Flapping & Outage Loop!
path: Lesson 26: Solving the GitOps Tug-of-War: KEDA + Argo CD Drift & Conflict Resolution

items.title: Why Does This Happen?
items.text:
1. Git is the Single Source of Truth: Your Git repository defines spec.replicas: 2.
  2. KEDA Dynamically Mutates the Live Object: When external events arrive, KEDA (or its managed HPA) mutates the live Deployment’s spec.replicas to 20.
  3. Argo CD Flags Drift: Argo CD compares Git against the live cluster state, detects that 2 != 20, marks the application as OutOfSync, and (if selfHeal: true is enabled) aggressively overwrites the replica count back to 2.
path: Lesson 26: Solving the GitOps Tug-of-War: KEDA + Argo CD Drift & Conflict Resolution

items.title: 2. The Solutions: Production Patterns
items.text: To solve the Replicas Tug-of-War, platform teams implement one or more of the following standard GitOps patterns.
path: Lesson 26: Solving the GitOps Tug-of-War: KEDA + Argo CD Drift & Conflict Resolution

items.title: Pattern 1: ignoreDifferences in Argo CD (Recommended)
items.text: The most robust and standard approach is instructing Argo CD to intentionally ignore mutations made to the /spec/replicas field of your workloads.
path: Lesson 26: Solving the GitOps Tug-of-War: KEDA + Argo CD Drift & Conflict Resolution

items.title: Option A: Application-Level Configuration
items.text:
Add ignoreDifferences directly to your Argo CD Application manifest:

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: payment-processor
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/my-org/gitops-apps.git
    targetRevision: HEAD
    path: apps/payment-processor
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: payments
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true                  # Safe to keep enabled now!
  ignoreDifferences:
    - group: apps
      kind: Deployment
      name: payment-worker            # Optional: omit to apply to all Deployments in app
      jsonPointers:
        - /spec/replicas
path: Lesson 26: Solving the GitOps Tug-of-War: KEDA + Argo CD Drift & Conflict Resolution

items.title: Option B: Global System-Wide Configuration
items.text:
If you have hundreds of autoscaled microservices, you can configure argocd-cm once so that Argo CD globally ignores spec.replicas on all Deployments managed by HPAs/KEDA:

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: argocd-cm
  namespace: argocd
data:
  resource.customizations.ignoreDifferences.apps_Deployment: |
    jsonPointers:
      - /spec/replicas
path: Lesson 26: Solving the GitOps Tug-of-War: KEDA + Argo CD Drift & Conflict Resolution

items.title: Pattern 2: Omitting spec.replicas from Git Manifests
items.text:
In Kubernetes, the spec.replicas field on a Deployment is optional and defaults to 1 when first created.

If you omit spec.replicas entirely from your YAML manifest in Git: 

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: payment-worker
spec:
  # Do NOT declare `replicas: 1` here!
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: payment-worker
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: payment-worker
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: worker
          image: my-registry/worker:v2.1.0
path: Lesson 26: Solving the GitOps Tug-of-War: KEDA + Argo CD Drift & Conflict Resolution

items.title: Why This Works:
items.text: When Argo CD performs a 3-way strategic merge patch, it compares only the fields declared in Git. Because spec.replicas is not defined in Git, Argo CD ignores whatever value KEDA writes to spec.replicas in the live cluster.
path: Lesson 26: Solving the GitOps Tug-of-War: KEDA + Argo CD Drift & Conflict Resolution

items.title: 3. Managing Auto-Generated HPAs & Extraneous Resources
items.text:
When you create a ScaledObject, KEDA automatically generates an underlying HorizontalPodAutoscaler object (named keda-hpa-<scaledobject-name>).

graph LR
    Git["Git Repo\n(Contains ScaledObject)"] -->|Synced by Argo CD| LiveSO["Live ScaledObject"]
    LiveSO -->|KEDA Controller Generates| GenHPA["keda-hpa-order-scaler\n(Extraneous Resource)"]
    Argo["Argo CD Sync with Pruning"] -.->|Must NOT delete!| GenHPA
path: Lesson 26: Solving the GitOps Tug-of-War: KEDA + Argo CD Drift & Conflict Resolution

items.title: Preventing Argo CD from Deleting KEDA's HPA
items.text:
Because the generated HPA does not exist in your Git repository, an overly aggressive Argo CD auto-prune policy might identify it as an "extraneous" resource.

  1. Never commit a manual HPA in Git if you are already declaring a KEDA ScaledObject. Having both causes two controllers to fight over the same deployment.
  2. KEDA assigns an ownerReference pointing to the parent ScaledObject. Argo CD recognizes this owner reference and will not prune the child HPA.
  3. If necessary, you can annotate resources or configure Argo CD to ignore extraneous resources: 
    metadata:
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/compare-options: IgnoreExtraneous
path: Lesson 26: Solving the GitOps Tug-of-War: KEDA + Argo CD Drift & Conflict Resolution

items.title: 4. KEDA Integration with Argo Rollouts
items.text:
For progressive canary and blue/green deployments, KEDA seamlessly targets the Rollout Custom Resource (argoproj.io/v1alpha1):

apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata:
  name: web-rollout-scaler
  namespace: frontend
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
    kind: Rollout                     # Target the Rollout CRD directly!
    name: web-app
  minReplicaCount: 2
  maxReplicaCount: 50
  triggers:
    - type: prometheus
      metadata:
        serverAddress: http://prometheus.monitoring.svc:9090
        metricName: http_requests_total
        query: sum(rate(http_requests_total{app="web-app"}[1m]))
        threshold: '50'

And in your Argo CD Application, ignore spec.replicas on the Rollout resource: 

ignoreDifferences:
  - group: argoproj.io
    kind: Rollout
    jsonPointers:
      - /spec/replicas
path: Lesson 26: Solving the GitOps Tug-of-War: KEDA + Argo CD Drift & Conflict Resolution

items.title: Test Your Knowledge
items.text:
1. What causes the destructive flapping cycle between Argo CD self-heal and KEDA?
  2. A) Argo CD reverts live replica changes because Git declares static replica counts
  3. B) KEDA operator crashes when Prometheus external queries exceed timeout limits

Answer: A) Argo CD reverts live replica changes because Git declares static replica counts - Correct! When Git specifies static replicas, Argo CD's self-healing reconciler treats KEDA's dynamic scaling as unauthorized drift and resets the replica count.

  1. What is the recommended Argo CD configuration to permit KEDA autoscaling while maintaining automated GitOps self-healing?
  2. A) Configure ignoreDifferences on /spec/replicas for the target Deployment
  3. B) Disable cluster RBAC permissions on the Argo CD application controller

Answer: A) Configure ignoreDifferences on /spec/replicas for the target Deployment - Correct! ignoreDifferences tells Argo CD to exclude the spec.replicas path from drift calculation, allowing KEDA full autonomy over replica scaling.
path: Lesson 26: Solving the GitOps Tug-of-War: KEDA + Argo CD Drift & Conflict Resolution

items.title: Lesson 27: Event-Driven Batch Processing with KEDA ScaledJobs & Secure Authentication
path: Lesson 27: Event-Driven Batch Processing with KEDA ScaledJobs & Secure Authentication

items.title: 1. When to Use ScaledJob vs. ScaledObject
items.text:
So far, we have scaled long-running servers using ScaledObject (Deployments, StatefulSets, and Argo Rollouts). However, many workloads are discrete, run-to-completion batch tasks: - Video & Media Transcoding: 1 video uploaded = 1 discrete transcoding Job. - Large Language Model (LLM) & AI Batch Inference: Processing heavy document embeddings. - Nightly Financial Settlement: Generating reports for each registered merchant. - Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ) Reprocessing: Replaying failed transactions one-by-one.

For these use cases, keeping warm pods running is wasteful. Instead, KEDA’s ScaledJob CRD dynamically spawns native Kubernetes Job objects that run to completion and terminate.

graph TD
    subgraph Queue["Message Queue (e.g., SQS / RabbitMQ)"]
        M1["Message 1: Process Video A"]
        M2["Message 2: Process Video B"]
        M3["Message 3: Process Video C"]
    end

    subgraph KEDA["KEDA Controller"]
        ScaledJob["ScaledJob Controller\n(Evaluates Queue Depth)"]
    end

    subgraph Cluster["Kubernetes Jobs (Run to Completion)"]
        Job1["K8s Job 1 (Pod A)\nProcesses Video A → Completes"]
        Job2["K8s Job 2 (Pod B)\nProcesses Video B → Completes"]
        Job3["K8s Job 3 (Pod C)\nProcesses Video C → Completes"]
    end

    Queue --> ScaledJob
    ScaledJob -->|Spawns 1 Job per Message| Job1
    ScaledJob -->|Spawns 1 Job per Message| Job2
    ScaledJob -->|Spawns 1 Job per Message| Job3
path: Lesson 27: Event-Driven Batch Processing with KEDA ScaledJobs & Secure Authentication

items.title: 2. Declarative ScaledJob Blueprint
items.text:
Here is a production ScaledJob that monitors an AWS SQS queue and spawns video transcoding jobs:

apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledJob
metadata:
  name: video-transcoder-scaledjob
  namespace: media-processing
spec:
  jobTargetRef:
    parallelism: 1                    # Pods per single job execution
    completions: 1                    # Successful pod runs needed to finish
    activeDeadlineSeconds: 1800       # Kill job if execution exceeds 30 minutes
    backoffLimit: 2                   # Max retries before marking job failed
    template:
      spec:
        restartPolicy: Never
        containers:
          - name: transcoder
            image: my-registry/video-transcoder:v1.4.0
            resources:
              requests:
                cpu: "2"
                memory: 4Gi
  pollingInterval: 10                 # Check SQS queue every 10 seconds
  maxReplicaCount: 50                 # Never exceed 50 concurrent active jobs
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 5       # Keep last 5 completed jobs for logs
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 10          # Keep last 10 failed jobs for debugging
  scalingStrategy:
    strategy: "accurate"              # 'default' or 'accurate' calculation
    targetWorkload: "1"               # 1 Job per 1 message in queue
  triggers:
    - type: aws-sqs-queue
      metadata:
        queueURL: https://sqs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/123456789012/video-uploads
        queueLength: "1"
        awsRegion: "us-east-1"
      authenticationRef:
        name: keda-aws-credentials    # Reference to TriggerAuthentication
path: Lesson 27: Event-Driven Batch Processing with KEDA ScaledJobs & Secure Authentication

items.title: 3. Secure Scaler Credentials: TriggerAuthentication
items.text:
Hardcoding credentials or access keys inside ScaledObject or ScaledJob manifests violates security best practices and exposes secrets in Git.

KEDA provides the TriggerAuthentication (namespace-scoped) and ClusterTriggerAuthentication (cluster-scoped) CRDs to decouple authentication.

graph LR
    SO["ScaledJob / ScaledObject"] -->|authenticationRef| TA["TriggerAuthentication"]
    TA -->|Method A: Workload Identity| CloudIAM["GCP WIF / AWS IRSA / Azure WI\n(Keyless Token Exchange)"]
    TA -->|Method B: Secret Reference| K8sSecret["Kubernetes Secret / Vault"]
path: Lesson 27: Event-Driven Batch Processing with KEDA ScaledJobs & Secure Authentication

items.title: Pattern A: Keyless Cloud Workload Identity (GCP WIF / AWS IRSA)
items.text:
In modern cloud clusters (GKE, EKS, AKS), the most secure approach uses Workload Identity so no static credentials ever touch the cluster.

apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: TriggerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: keda-gcp-credentials
  namespace: media-processing
spec:
  podIdentity:
    provider: gcp                     # Keyless GCP Workload Identity
path: Lesson 27: Event-Driven Batch Processing with KEDA ScaledJobs & Secure Authentication

items.title: Pattern B: Kubernetes Secret Reference
items.text:
If using API tokens or database passwords:

apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: TriggerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: keda-db-credentials
  namespace: analytics
spec:
  secretTargetRef:
    - parameter: connectionString     # Name expected by the KEDA scaler
      name: postgres-secret           # Kubernetes Secret name
      key: DB_CONNECTION_URL          # Key inside the Secret
path: Lesson 27: Event-Driven Batch Processing with KEDA ScaledJobs & Secure Authentication

items.title: 4. Production Resilience & Cleanups
items.text:
When designing event-driven batch jobs, enforce these best practices:

  1. Set successfulJobsHistoryLimit & failedJobsHistoryLimit: Kubernetes stores finished Job metadata in etcd. Failing to set history limits will accumulate thousands of dead Job objects and degrade API server performance.
  2. Set activeDeadlineSeconds: Prevents rogue or hanging batch jobs from running indefinitely and exhausting cluster compute or cloud budgets.
  3. Idempotency & Dead-Letter Queues (DLQ): Ensure batch jobs can safely retry without creating duplicate side-effects (e.g. charging a credit card twice). If a message crashes a job repeatedly, move it to a DLQ.
path: Lesson 27: Event-Driven Batch Processing with KEDA ScaledJobs & Secure Authentication

items.title: Test Your Knowledge
items.text:
1. When should you choose a ScaledJob instead of a ScaledObject?
  2. A) For discrete batch tasks that process an event and run to completion
  3. B) For long-running HTTP microservices that accept live incoming connections

Answer: A) For discrete batch tasks that process an event and run to completion - Correct! ScaledJob is engineered for run-to-completion batch workloads (e.g., video transcoding, report generation), whereas ScaledObject manages long-running servers.

  1. Why is using TriggerAuthentication with Cloud Workload Identity preferred over static API keys in GitOps?
  2. A) It eliminates static credentials and uses short-lived cryptographic tokens
  3. B) It automatically compiles application source code before scaling pods

Answer: A) It eliminates static credentials and uses short-lived cryptographic tokens - Correct! Workload Identity (GCP WIF, AWS IRSA) allows KEDA to authenticate to external cloud APIs keylessly without storing plaintext secrets in Git.
path: Lesson 27: Event-Driven Batch Processing with KEDA ScaledJobs & Secure Authentication
